items.stemEs: Lee el siguiente fragmento de un artículo periodístico de 1932: 'En los pueblos cercanos a las puertas de las fábricas, las familias han construido asentamientos de cartón, hojalata y madera de desecho. Hombres que antes ganaban salarios estables forman colas que se extienden alrededor de las manzanas de la ciudad, esperando un plato de sopa.' ¿Qué conclusión sobre el impacto social de la Gran Depresión está MEJOR respaldada por este relato?

choices.text: The Depression caused mass unemployment that stripped previously employed workers of economic stability, forcing those who had lived modest working-class lives into poverty and homelessness.
choices.textEs: La Depresión causó un desempleo masivo que despojó a los trabajadores previamente empleados de su estabilidad económica, obligando a quienes habían llevado una vida modesta de clase trabajadora a caer en la pobreza y la falta de hogar.

choices.text: Hoovervilles and breadlines were evidence that President Hoover had completely failed to respond to the Depression, which caused public opinion to turn sharply against him by 1932.

La evidencia apunta al colapso de la clase trabajadora previamente empleada.

items.stem: Between 1930 and 1933, unemployment in the United States rose from approximately 3% to nearly 25%. A student argues this figure understates the true human impact of the Depression. Which reasoning most effectively supports this argument?
items.stemEs: Entre 1930 y 1933, el desempleo en Estados Unidos aumentó de aproximadamente el 3% al casi 25%. Un estudiante argumenta que esta cifra subestima el verdadero impacto humano de la Depresión. ¿Qué razonamiento apoya más eficazmente este argumento?

choices.text: Unemployment statistics do not capture underemployment, wage cuts, or reduced hours, so many millions of technically employed workers also suffered severe economic hardship during the Depression.
choices.textEs: Las estadísticas de desempleo no capturan el subempleo, los recortes salariales ni la reducción de horas, por lo que muchos millones de trabajadores técnicamente empleados también sufrieron graves penurias económicas durante la Depresión.

choices.text: Unemployment statistics were inaccurate during the Depression because the federal government lacked the bureaucratic infrastructure to count unemployed workers accurately in rural areas.
choices.textEs: Las estadísticas de desempleo eran inexactas durante la Depresión porque el gobierno federal carecía de la infraestructura burocrática para contar con precisión a los trabajadores desempleados en las zonas rurales.

choices.text: The official unemployment figure excluded African Americans and women, who were disproportionately affected by job losses during the Depression but were not counted in official labor statistics.
choices.textEs: La cifra oficial de desempleo excluía a los afroamericanos y las mujeres, quienes se vieron afectados desproporcionadamente por las pérdidas de empleo durante la Depresión, pero no estaban incluidos en las estadísticas laborales oficiales.

choices.text: The 25% figure measures only urban industrial unemployment; if rural and agricultural unemployment had been included, the true rate would have been closer to 40% of the American workforce.
choices.textEs: La cifra del 25% mide solo el desempleo industrial urbano; si se hubiera incluido el desempleo rural y agrícola, la tasa real habría sido cercana al 40% de la fuerza laboral estadounidense.

items.explanation: The unemployment rate captures only those without jobs, not those working part-time when they need full-time work (underemployment), those who have given up looking (discouraged workers), or those who accepted dramatic wage cuts to keep jobs. Additionally, for the millions who remained employed, wage cuts, reduced hours, and fear of job loss drastically altered living standards and psychological well-being. The human impact therefore extended far beyond the 25% figure, which understates total economic suffering. This requires students to critically evaluate the limits of a quantitative measure — a DOK 3 task.
items.explanationEs: La tasa de desempleo captura solo a los que no tienen trabajo, no a los que trabajan a tiempo parcial cuando necesitan tiempo completo (subempleo), a los que han renunciado a buscar trabajo (trabajadores desanimados), o a los que aceptaron recortes salariales drásticos para mantener sus empleos. Además, para los millones que permanecieron empleados, los recortes salariales, la reducción de horas y el miedo a perder el trabajo alteraron drásticamente los niveles de vida y el bienestar psicológico.

items.stem: During the Great Depression, approximately 2 million Americans became transients, riding freight trains and moving from city to city in search of work. A historian argues this mass migration was economically and socially self-defeating. Which reasoning BEST supports this interpretation?
items.stemEs: Durante la Gran Depresión, aproximadamente 2 millones de estadounidenses se convirtieron en vagabundos, viajando en trenes de carga y moviéndose de ciudad en ciudad en busca de trabajo. Un historiador argumenta que esta migración masiva era económica y socialmente contraproducente. ¿Qué razonamiento apoya MEJOR esta interpretación?

choices.text: Because transients rode freight trains illegally, they were frequently arrested and jailed, which created a new underclass of criminalized poor people who could no longer find legitimate employment.
choices.textEs: Debido a que los vagabundos viajaban ilegalmente en trenes de carga, eran frecuentemente arrestados y encarcelados, lo que creó una nueva subclase de pobres criminalizados que ya no podían encontrar empleo legítimo.

choices.text: Moving from city to city spread infectious diseases, creating public health crises that overwhelmed the already-strained medical infrastructure of Depression-era cities.
choices.textEs: Moverse de ciudad en ciudad propagó enfermedades infecciosas, creando crisis de salud pública que desbordaron la ya sobrecargada infraestructura médica de las ciudades de la era de la Depresión.

choices.text: Transient workers competed directly with established residents for the same jobs, generating racial and ethnic conflicts that permanently damaged social relations in many American cities.
choices.textEs: Los trabajadores itinerantes competían directamente con los residentes establecidos por los mismos empleos, generando conflictos raciales y étnicos que dañaron permanentemente las relaciones sociales en muchas ciudades estadounidenses.

choices.text: Moving increased the supply of labor wherever migrants arrived, depressing wages even further, while also cutting transients off from family support networks and local relief programs that required residency to access.
choices.textEs: La migración aumentaba la oferta de trabajo dondequiera que llegaban los migrantes, deprimiendo aún más los salarios, y al mismo tiempo desconectaba a los vagabundos de las redes de apoyo familiar y los programas de ayuda local que requerían residencia para acceder a ellos.

items.explanation: Mass transience was self-defeating because it concentrated large numbers of job-seekers in the same cities simultaneously, increasing labor supply and depressing wages. At the same time, it broke the social bonds of community and family, removing individuals from the mutual aid networks that might have otherwise helped them survive. Arriving unknown in a new city, transients faced discrimination, lack of local social services, and were disqualified from local relief programs that required residency. The historian's point is that movement itself undermined the very goals (work, stability) migrants were seeking. This requires multi-step inferential reasoning.
items.explanationEs: La migración masiva era contraproducente porque concentraba grandes cantidades de solicitantes de empleo en las mismas ciudades simultáneamente, aumentando la oferta de trabajo y deprimiendo los salarios. Al mismo tiempo, rompía los lazos sociales de comunidad y familia, alejando a los individuos de las redes de ayuda mutua que de otro modo podrían haberles ayudado a sobrevivir. Los vagabundos que llegaban desconocidos a una nueva ciudad enfrentaban discriminación y falta de servicios sociales locales.

items.stem: A student compares two photographs: one shows a middle-class family's home in 1928, and the second shows the same family in a Hooverville shelter in 1932. The student concludes that the Hooverville was evidence that the government had failed the American people. A second student argues the photographs are primarily evidence of the scale of economic collapse. Which argument is better supported by the photographic evidence alone?
items.stemEs: Un estudiante compara dos fotografías: una muestra el hogar de una familia de clase media en 1928, y la segunda muestra a la misma familia en un refugio de Hooverville en 1932. El estudiante concluye que el Hooverville era evidencia de que el gobierno había fallado al pueblo americano. Un segundo estudiante argumenta que las fotografías son principalmente evidencia de la escala del colapso económico. ¿Qué argumento está mejor respaldado únicamente por la evidencia fotográfica?

choices.text: The first student's argument is better supported because the name 'Hooverville' itself is evidence that Americans blamed the government for their suffering.
choices.textEs: El argumento del primer estudiante está mejor respaldado porque el nombre 'Hooverville' en sí mismo es evidencia de que los estadounidenses culpaban al gobierno de su sufrimiento.

choices.text: The second student's argument is better supported because the photographs document the scale of economic collapse directly, while the government-failure interpretation requires evidence beyond what the images themselves show.
choices.textEs: El argumento del segundo estudiante está mejor respaldado porque las fotografías documentan directamente la escala del colapso económico, mientras que la interpretación del fracaso gubernamental requiere evidencia más allá de lo que las imágenes por sí mismas muestran.

choices.text: Both arguments are equally well supported because photographs of suffering inevitably raise questions about government responsibility, making both conclusions valid inferences from the same evidence.
choices.textEs: Ambos argumentos están igualmente bien respaldados porque las fotografías del sufrimiento inevitablemente plantean preguntas sobre la responsabilidad del gobierno, haciendo que ambas conclusiones sean inferencias válidas de la misma evidencia.

choices.text: Neither argument is well supported because photographs are subjective documents that cannot provide reliable evidence about either the scale of economic collapse or the adequacy of government response.
choices.textEs: Ninguno de los argumentos está bien respaldado porque las fotografías son documentos subjetivos que no pueden proporcionar evidencia confiable sobre la escala del colapso económico ni sobre la adecuación de la respuesta gubernamental.

items.explanation: The photographs alone show the scale of economic devastation — a family's dramatic fall from stability to destitution. They do not, by themselves, show why the fall happened, what the government did or didn't do, or whether policy could have prevented it. The government-failure interpretation requires additional evidence about government actions and inactions. The photographs are primary evidence of economic magnitude, not of government culpability. Students must evaluate what evidence can and cannot support — a core DOK 3 source analysis skill.
items.explanationEs: Las fotografías por sí solas muestran la escala de la devastación económica: la dramática caída de una familia de la estabilidad a la indigencia. Por sí mismas, no muestran por qué ocurrió la caída, qué hizo o no hizo el gobierno, ni si la política podría haberlo evitado. La interpretación del fracaso gubernamental requiere evidencia adicional sobre las acciones e inacciones del gobierno. Las fotografías son evidencia primaria de la magnitud económica, no de la culpabilidad del gobierno.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from Franklin D. Roosevelt's Second Inaugural Address, January 20, 1937 (National Archives, public domain):

"I see one-third of a nation ill-housed, ill-clad, ill-nourished... The test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little."

Using this source and your knowledge of the New Deal, construct an argument that evaluates the tension between FDR's vision of government responsibility and the limits placed on that vision by his critics and the Supreme Court. In your response:
1. Identify the governing philosophy expressed in this excerpt and explain how at least TWO specific New Deal programs embodied that philosophy.
2. Explain at least TWO specific criticisms of the New Deal from the political right OR left (e.g., Huey Long, Father Coughlin, the Supreme Court in Schechter Poultry v. United States, or business leaders).
3. Evaluate the extent to which these criticisms forced FDR to modify or defend his vision of government's role in the economy.

Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente fragmento del Segundo Discurso Inaugural de Franklin D. Roosevelt, 20 de enero de 1937 (Archivos Nacionales, dominio público):

'Veo a un tercio de una nación mal alojado, mal vestido, mal alimentado... La prueba de nuestro progreso no es si añadimos más a la abundancia de los que tienen mucho; es si proporcionamos lo suficiente para los que tienen demasiado poco.'

Usando esta fuente y su conocimiento del New Deal, construya un argumento que evalúe la tensión entre la visión de FDR sobre la responsabilidad del gobierno y los límites impuestos a esa visión por sus críticos y la Corte Suprema. En su respuesta:
1. Identifique la filosofía de gobierno expresada en este fragmento y explique cómo al menos DOS programas específicos del New Deal embodied esa filosofía.
2. Explique al menos DOS críticas específicas del New Deal desde la derecha O izquierda política (p. ej., Huey Long, Father Coughlin, la Corte Suprema en Schechter Poultry v. United States, o líderes empresariales).
3. Evalúe en qué medida estas críticas obligaron a FDR a modificar o defender su visión del papel del gobierno en la economía.

Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4-point) response will: (1) Identify FDR's philosophy as active federal responsibility for the economic welfare of citizens — a departure from laissez-faire orthodoxy — and connect it to specific programs such as the Social Security Act (1935, providing old-age insurance and unemployment compensation), the Works Progress Administration (employing 8.5 million in public works), the Agricultural Adjustment Act (price supports for farmers), or the Second New Deal's focus on redistribution. (2) Present at least two substantive criticisms: Huey Long's 'Share Our Wealth' plan (criticizing FDR from the left as insufficiently redistributive, proposing a $5,000 annual family income guarantee); Father Coughlin's anti-New Deal radio broadcasts reaching 40 million listeners; the Supreme Court striking down NIRA (Schechter Poultry, 1935) and AAA (Butler, 1936) on constitutional grounds; or business coalition opposition via the American Liberty League. (3) Evaluate modification: FDR responded to critics by pivoting from the First to the Second New Deal (more redistributive legislation, Wagner Act, Social Security), and later by proposing the Court-packing plan (1937) when the Supreme Court blocked his programs — demonstrating that he defended his vision while tactically adapting to political pressure. CER structure must be explicit throughout.
items.dokRationale: Student must evaluate a primary source text by FDR to synthesize the philosophical underpinnings of the New Deal (US.41) against the constitutional and ideological critiques it generated (US.44), requiring extended cross-standard analysis and argument construction.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from the Tennessee Valley Authority Act, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on May 18, 1933 (National Archives, public domain):

"Be it enacted...that there is hereby created a body corporate by the name of the 'Tennessee Valley Authority'...The President is authorized...to construct dams, reservoirs, power houses, power structures, transmission lines, navigation projects, and incidental works in the Tennessee River and its tributaries...for the especial purpose of bringing about in said Tennessee Valley...the maximum amount of flood control; the maximum development...of said Tennessee River for navigation purposes; the maximum generation of electric power consistent with flood control and navigation; [and] the proper use of marginal lands."

Using this source and your knowledge of the Tennessee Valley Authority, construct an argument that evaluates the TVA as BOTH a regional development project for Tennessee AND as a model for the broader New Deal philosophy of federal intervention. In your response:
1. Identify the multiple, simultaneous purposes of the TVA as expressed in the Act, and explain why a multi-purpose federal agency was a significant departure from earlier approaches to economic development.
2. Explain at least TWO specific ways the TVA transformed life in Tennessee and the broader Tennessee Valley by the late 1930s.
3. Evaluate the extent to which the TVA's model — federal ownership of power production — made it the most ideologically controversial element of the New Deal.

Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente fragmento de la Ley de la Autoridad del Valle de Tennessee, firmada por el Presidente Franklin D. Roosevelt el 18 de mayo de 1933 (Archivos Nacionales, dominio público):

'Sea promulgado...que se crea por este medio una corporación con el nombre de "Autoridad del Valle de Tennessee"...El Presidente está autorizado...para construir represas, embalses, plantas de energía, estructuras de energía, líneas de transmisión, proyectos de navegación y obras incidentales en el río Tennessee y sus afluentes...con el propósito especial de lograr en dicho Valle de Tennessee...el máximo de control de inundaciones; el máximo desarrollo...del río Tennessee para fines de navegación; la máxima generación de energía eléctrica consistente con el control de inundaciones y la navegación; [y] el uso apropiado de tierras marginales.'

Usando esta fuente y su conocimiento de la Autoridad del Valle de Tennessee, construya un argumento que evalúe la TVA como TANTO un proyecto de desarrollo regional para Tennessee COMO un modelo para la filosofía más amplia del New Deal de intervención federal. En su respuesta:
1. Identifique los múltiples propósitos simultáneos de la TVA expresados en la Ley, y explique por qué una agencia federal multipropósito fue una desviación significativa de enfoques anteriores al desarrollo económico.
2. Explique al menos DOS formas específicas en que la TVA transformó la vida en Tennessee y el Valle de Tennessee más amplio para finales de la década de 1930.
3. Evalúe en qué medida el modelo de la TVA — propiedad federal de la producción de energía — lo convirtió en el elemento más ideológicamente controvertido del New Deal.

Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4-point) response will: (1) Identify the TVA Act's multi-purpose mandate — flood control, navigation improvement, electric power generation, and land conservation — and connect this integrated approach to the New Deal's departure from laissez-faire economics, noting that the federal government was now directly owning and operating power infrastructure in competition with private utilities. (2) Provide at least two specific Tennessee-centered impacts: electrification of rural Tennessee communities (by 1940, TVA provided electricity to farms and homes that private companies had deemed unprofitable to serve); construction of Norris Dam (1936) and other dams controlling Tennessee River flooding that had repeatedly devastated agricultural communities; reduction in electricity rates that stimulated industrial development; soil conservation programs and erosion control on marginal Tennessee farmland; and improved river navigation opening commerce. (3) Evaluate ideological controversy: the TVA's direct government ownership of power production was attacked by private utilities and conservative critics as 'socialism' and unconstitutional federal overreach; it survived a Supreme Court challenge (Ashwander v. TVA, 1936) and became the most enduring regulatory model of the New Deal era, provoking debates about public vs. private power that persisted for decades. CER structure explicit throughout.

DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze the three primary sources below. Then respond to the prompt using evidence from ALL THREE documents and your own historical knowledge.

---
DOCUMENT A
Tennessee Valley Authority Act, Section 1, May 18, 1933 (National Archives, public domain):
"Be it enacted...for the especial purpose of bringing about in said Tennessee Valley and adjoining territory...the maximum amount of flood control; the maximum development of said Tennessee River for navigation purposes; the maximum generation of electric power consistent with flood control and navigation; the proper use of marginal lands; the proper method of reforestation of all lands in said drainage basin suitable for reforestation; and the economic and social well-being of the people living in said river basin."

---
DOCUMENT B
FDR Message to Congress Recommending Establishment of the TVA, April 10, 1933 (FDR Presidential Library, public domain):
"It is clear that the Muscle Shoals development is but a small part of the potential public usefulness of the entire Tennessee River...if we are careful and far-sighted, we can make it serve as a model for the whole nation... I suggest that this power development of war days be used not merely as an opportunity for the comfort and happiness of adjoining States but as a means of planning for the improvement of the broadest of physical, social, and economic conditions in the whole of the territory."

---
DOCUMENT C
Statement of Wendell Willkie, President of Commonwealth and Southern Corporation (private utility), opposing TVA expansion, Congressional testimony, 1933 (Congressional Record, public domain):
"The Tennessee Valley Authority is entering into direct competition with established private industry which has made enormous investments in good faith under the laws of the land. The power business is not a natural monopoly...The government should not compete with private enterprise in the distribution of electric power. This is not a question of power rates; it is a question of whether the government of the United States is going to socialize the electric utility industry."

---
PROMPT: Using all three documents and your knowledge of the Tennessee Valley Authority (1933–1941) and the broader New Deal debate, construct an argument that answers: To what extent did the TVA represent a new model for the relationship between the federal government and regional economic development — and why was it so ideologically contested?

In your response, you MUST:
1. Analyze each document using the HIPP framework — identify at least ONE HIPP element for each document (historical context, intended audience, purpose, or point of view).
2. Identify the purpose and scope of the TVA as presented in Documents A and B, and explain what made this vision of federal intervention genuinely new.
3. Evaluate Willkie's critique (Document C) using historical evidence — was his characterization of the TVA as 'socialization' accurate, and what does this debate reveal about the limits of the New Deal consensus?
4. Use at least two pieces of outside historical knowledge to strengthen your argument about the TVA's historical significance in Tennessee and nationally.

'La organización de un organismo no partidista...para defender y mantener la Constitución...para enseñar la necesidad de respetar los derechos de las personas y la propiedad como fundamento de toda forma de gobierno...La Liga fue formada para combatir lo que sus fundadores creían que era una extensión inconstitucional del poder federal que amenazaba el sistema estadounidense de libre empresa y libertad individual.'

DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze the three primary sources below. Then respond to the prompt using evidence from ALL THREE documents and your own historical knowledge.

---
DOCUMENT A
National Industrial Recovery Act, Section 1 (Declaration of Policy), June 16, 1933 (National Archives, public domain):
"A national emergency productive of widespread unemployment and disorganization of industry, which burdens interstate and foreign commerce...is hereby declared to exist. It is hereby declared to be the policy of Congress to remove obstructions to the free flow of interstate and foreign commerce which tend to diminish the amount thereof; and to provide for the general welfare by promoting the organization of industry for the purpose of cooperative action among trade groups..."

---
DOCUMENT B
National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act), Section 1 (Findings and Policy), July 5, 1935 (National Archives, public domain):
"The inequality of bargaining power between employees who do not possess full freedom of association or actual liberty of contract, and employers who are organized in the corporate or other forms of ownership association substantially burdens and affects the flow of commerce...It is hereby declared to be the policy of the United States to eliminate the causes of certain substantial obstructions to the free flow of commerce...by protecting the exercise by workers of full freedom of association, self-organization, and designation of representatives of their own choosing."

---
DOCUMENT C
FDR, Message to Congress on Tax Revision, June 19, 1935 (FDR Presidential Library, public domain):
"Our revenue laws have operated in many ways to the unfair advantage of the few, and they have done little to prevent an unjust concentration of wealth and economic power...The very wealthy may be able to hire the ablest tax lawyers so that the letter of the tax law is followed but not the spirit...Inherited economic power is as inconsistent with the ideals of this generation as inherited political power was inconsistent with the ideals of the generation which established our Government."

---
PROMPT: Using all three documents and your knowledge of the New Deal (1933–1938), construct an argument that answers: How did the New Deal evolve from the First New Deal (1933–1934) to the Second New Deal (1935–1938), and what does this evolution reveal about FDR's response to political pressure from critics on both the left and right?

In your response, you MUST:
1. Analyze each document using the HIPP framework — at least ONE HIPP element per document.
2. Place each document within the First or Second New Deal phase and explain what governing philosophy it reflects.
3. Construct a central argument using all three documents AND at least two outside historical facts explaining how the shift from Document A to Documents B and C reflects a meaningful philosophical and political evolution in the New Deal.
4. Evaluate: Was the Second New Deal a genuine ideological shift toward redistribution and worker empowerment, or primarily a political strategy to neutralize critics like Huey Long and the Supreme Court?

Extended Response — No sources are provided for this question. Draw entirely on your knowledge of U.S. history.

The New Deal of the 1930s generated one of the most consequential debates in American political history: a debate about what the Constitution permits the federal government to do in response to an economic emergency. Critics came from across the political spectrum — some arguing FDR had done too little, others insisting he had done too much or had violated the constitutional separation of powers.

Write an extended response that constructs and defends an argument in answer to the following question:

To what extent did the critics of the New Deal — from the left, the right, and the judiciary — collectively shape the boundaries of American government's power over the economy, both during the 1930s and as a lasting constitutional and political legacy?

Your response MUST:
1. State a clear, specific, and defensible claim about the collective impact of New Deal critics on the scope and direction of American government power.
2. Address at least THREE distinct critics or categories of criticism (e.g., Huey Long, Father Coughlin, the American Liberty League, the Supreme Court's 'Four Horsemen,' or state-level opponents) with specific, accurate historical evidence about each.
3. Explain how FDR's response to these critics — including specific policy pivots, legislative strategies, or institutional confrontations — demonstrated the interaction between criticism and governance.
4. Evaluate the lasting constitutional or political legacy of the New Deal debate about government's economic role — connecting this debate to at least ONE later moment in U.S. history (post-1945) when the same fundamental tension re-emerged.

Use the CER (Claim-Evidence-Reasoning) framework throughout.

Respuesta Extendida — No se proporcionan fuentes para esta pregunta. Basa tu respuesta completamente en tu conocimiento de la historia de los EE.UU.

El New Deal de la década de 1930 generó uno de los debates más consecuentes en la historia política estadounidense: un debate sobre lo que la Constitución permite al gobierno federal hacer en respuesta a una emergencia económica. Los críticos vinieron de todo el espectro político — algunos argumentando que FDR había hecho muy poco, otros insistiendo en que había hecho demasiado o había violado la separación constitucional de poderes.

Escriba una respuesta extendida que construya y defienda un argumento en respuesta a la siguiente pregunta:

¿En qué medida los críticos del New Deal — de izquierda, derecha y el poder judicial — moldearon colectivamente los límites del poder del gobierno estadounidense sobre la economía, tanto durante la década de 1930 como como legado constitucional y político duradero?

Su respuesta DEBE:
1. Enunciar una afirmación clara, específica y defendible sobre el impacto colectivo de los críticos del New Deal en el alcance y dirección del poder del gobierno estadounidense.
2. Abordar al menos TRES críticos distintos o categorías de crítica (p. ej., Huey Long, Father Coughlin, la Liga Americana por la Libertad, los 'Cuatro Jinetes' de la Corte Suprema, u opositores a nivel estatal) con evidencia histórica específica y precisa sobre cada uno.
3. Explicar cómo la respuesta de FDR a estos críticos — incluyendo giros específicos de política, estrategias legislativas o confrontaciones institucionales — demostró la interacción entre la crítica y la gobernanza.
4. Evaluar el legado constitucional o político duradero del debate del New Deal sobre el papel económico del gobierno — conectando este debate con al menos UN momento posterior en la historia de los EE.UU. (después de 1945) cuando la misma tensión fundamental reemergió.

Use el marco CER (Afirmación-Evidencia-Razonamiento) a lo largo de su respuesta.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4-point) extended response will: (1) CLAIM: A defensible, nuanced claim — e.g., 'The critics of the New Deal — from Huey Long on the left, the American Liberty League on the right, and the Supreme Court's Four Horsemen in the judiciary — collectively forced FDR to both expand and constrain his vision of federal economic power, producing a constitutional settlement that expanded federal authority significantly while establishing limits that persisted for decades. The debate's lasting legacy is the still-unresolved tension between democratic demand for economic security and constitutional limits on federal economic intervention.' (2) THREE CRITICS with specific evidence: Huey Long: Share Our Wealth program (1934–1935), proposing to cap individual fortunes at $3 million and guarantee every family $5,000 annual income; 4.5 million Share Our Wealth club members by 1935; Long's threat as an independent presidential candidate pushed FDR to the left and directly influenced the Second New Deal's Revenue Act of 1935 and Social Security Act. Long was assassinated September 8, 1935. Father Coughlin: National Union for Social Justice (1934); weekly radio broadcasts reaching 40 million listeners; initially pro-New Deal but turned sharply anti-FDR by 1936, attacking him as insufficiently anti-banker; Coughlin's movement revealed the depth of populist frustration that the New Deal was managing but not fully satisfying. The Supreme Court 'Four Horsemen' (Van Devanter, McReynolds, Sutherland, Butler): struck down NIRA in Schechter Poultry v. United States (1935) and AAA in United States v. Butler (1936); their constitutional originalism forced FDR to redesign key programs; FDR's response — the Court-packing plan (February 1937, proposing to add one justice for each sitting justice over 70, up to six) — failed in Congress but produced the 'switch in time that saved nine' (Justice Owen Roberts shifting to uphold New Deal laws in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish, 1937). American Liberty League: founded 1934, backed by Du Pont and General Motors executives; argued New Deal was unconstitutional socialism; published legal briefs, funded court cases, supported Republican opposition. (3) FDR's responses: Second New Deal pivot (1935) as response to left critics; Court-packing plan as response to judicial critics (1937); Social Security designed with payroll tax financing specifically to make it constitutionally defensible and politically irreversible. (4) Lasting constitutional legacy: The New Deal constitutional settlement established that the Commerce Clause permits broad federal economic regulation (NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel, 1937). This was challenged again during the Reagan Revolution (1980s — deregulation, supply-side economics as rejection of New Deal regulatory state) and in the Affordable Care Act litigation (NFIB v. Sebelius, 2012, where Chief Justice Roberts upheld ACA under the taxing power while limiting Commerce Clause expansion). CER explicit throughout.
